title: Reservoir Computing with Heterogeneous Magnetic Metamaterials
authors: R. Yagan, C. Swindells, I. T. Vidamour, G. Venkat, J. C. Gartside, E. Vasilaki, M. O. A. Ellis, T. J. Hayward
abstract: Physical reservoir computing utilizes the intrinsic nonlinear and history-dependent dynamics of physical systems to perform machine-learning tasks with minimal training overhead. Here, we introduce a nanomagnetic reservoir computer based on a heterogeneous array of interconnected magnetic nanorings, combined with multi-channel planar Hall effect readout. The device comprises subarrays of rings with systematically varied track widths ranging from 500 nm to 300 nm, enabling access to the heterogeneous dynamics of geometrically diverse magnetic systems within a single reservoir. By applying time-varying input signals as modulations of a driving rotating magnetic field, we evaluate the nanoring reservoir's performance on nonlinear signal transformation and Mackey-Glass time-series prediction tasks. We find that combining outputs from multiple width-dependent channels significantly reduces the normalized root-mean-square error compared to single-channel readout, with the optimal channel combinations depending on task requirements. These results demonstrate that geometric heterogeneity provides an additional, experimentally accessible degree of freedom and complementary computational features. Principal component analysis further reveals that a reduced subset of correlated features captures most of the computationally relevant information while suppressing noise contributions. These results demonstrate that controlled geometric heterogeneity enhances reservoir expressivity and suggest a route toward scalable magnetic computing architectures in which multi-output magnetic metamaterials serve as configurable dynamical building blocks for device networks.
summary: The paper develops and tests a nanomagnetic reservoir computer using heterogeneous magnetic nanorings. By reading out signals from multiple channels corresponding to different ring widths, the authors show that geometric disorder enhances the system's computational capacity for tasks like time-series prediction. This suggests a scalable route toward magnetic neuromorphic computing.
main_problem: The research aims to utilize the intrinsic nonlinear dynamics of physical magnetic systems for machine learning tasks, specifically reservoir computing, minimizing external training overhead.
main_result: Combining outputs from multiple geometrically heterogeneous channels significantly enhances the reservoir's expressivity and computational performance compared to single-channel readouts.
method: The authors tested the system on nonlinear signal transformation (SigT) and Mackey-Glass time-series prediction (MG-TSP) using multi-channel planar Hall effect readout combined with Principal Component Analysis (PCA).
model_or_system: The platform is a nanomagnetic reservoir computer built from an array of interconnected magnetic nanorings whose track widths are systematically varied across the device. The dynamics are governed by domain-wall motion modulated by a rotating external magnetic field.
key_observables: Normalized Root-Mean-Square Error (NRMSE) for prediction tasks, explained variance ratio from PCA, and PHE signals measured at $1f$ and $2f$.
important_parameters: Ring track widths ranging from 500 nm to 300 nm; input modulation fields ($H_0$, $H_r$).
main_assumptions: The improvements in performance are attributed to genuinely diverse feature sets provided by multiple channels, rather than just an increase in trainable parameters.

paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical basis (nanomagnetic reservoir) and then systematically evaluates its performance on two distinct ML tasks, using multi-channel readout and dimensionality reduction techniques (PCA) to quantify the benefit of geometric heterogeneity.
why_interesting: This work demonstrates a concrete pathway for integrating concepts from condensed matter physics (magnetic domain dynamics in metamaterials) directly into computational hardware architectures, providing an experimental realization of physical computation principles relevant to open quantum systems modeling.
